zh: 最终长度可能是天文数字，不能真的展开字符串。注意每个字母的后代只取决于它自己是哪个字母：同一字母的所有副本演化完全相同，所以只需要记录 26 个字母各有多少个。
一轮转换中，字母 a..y 各变成下一个字母，z 变成 a 和 b 各一个；这是作用在 26 维计数向量上的线性变换，可以写成 26×26 的转移矩阵 M。t 轮之后的计数向量就是 M^t 乘初始向量，t 可达 2^31−1，必须用矩阵快速幂而不能逐轮迭代。
逐字节扫描第一行，统计 26 个字母的个数（不必保存整串）；读入 t。构造 M：对 i<25 令 M[i+1][i]=1，再令 M[0][25]=M[1][25]=1。用二进制快速幂求 M^t（t=0 时为单位阵），每次乘加后立即对 1000000007 取模，中间值用 64 位整数。答案为所有 i、j 上 M^t[i][j]·count[j] 之和取模；空串自然得到 0。
en: The final length can be astronomically large, so you cannot actually expand the string. Notice that the descendants of a letter depend only on which letter it is: every copy of the same letter evolves identically, so you only need to know how many of each of the 26 letters there are.

In one round, each letter a..y becomes the next letter, and z becomes one a and one b; this is a linear transformation on the 26-dimensional count vector and can be written as a 26×26 transition matrix M. The count vector after t rounds is M^t times the initial vector, and since t can be as large as 2^31−1, you must use fast matrix exponentiation rather than iterating round by round.

Scan the first line byte by byte and count each of the 26 letters (there is no need to keep the whole string), then read t. Build M: set M[i+1][i]=1 for i<25, and set M[0][25]=M[1][25]=1. Compute M^t with binary exponentiation (the identity matrix when t=0), reducing modulo 1000000007 right after every multiply-add and keeping intermediate values in 64-bit integers. The answer is the sum of M^t[i][j]·count[j] over all i and j, modulo 1000000007; an empty string naturally gives 0.

explanationEn:
## Original rules, completed example and disclosure of ranges

fastprep/BNY Mellon/bnymellon-calculate-string-transformations-length.md at the fixed commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc explains that in every round each original character of the string is replaced: z becomes ab, and every other lowercase letter becomes the next letter. The statement explicitly says that azbk becomes babcl after one round, which is enough to prove that new characters produced in a round cannot be transformed again in the same round; the old blocking reason, that the simultaneous semantics were unclear, does not hold.

The first public example comes from the statement's azbk,t=1, whose result babcl has length 5; the second keeps the original example input abczy,t=2: the first round gives bcdabz and the second round should give cdebcab, length 7. The original output field says TO-DO rather than an original answer that could be kept, and the original explanation of the second round drops the z and gives the wrong string cdedbc. This site explicitly states that 7 was filled in by derivation from the original rules, and does not falsely claim that the original text provided 7. The third public example, z,t=0, is a boundary case added by this site.

The original text gives no numeric constraints. t follows the original Java interface int combined with a non-negative number of transformations and is interpreted as 0..2147483647; this is derived from the type and the semantics, not a decimal constraint listed in the original. word consists of lowercase English letters; this site does not invent an extra length cap of 100000 and instead covers every transmittable string within the existing 32MiB standard input budget per case. An empty word is also accepted and returns 0, which is explicitly this site's mathematical extension to the empty string. The input is exactly two lines: word, then t; an empty first line is the empty string. The output is the mathematical length modulo 1000000007; there is no need to output the actual exponentially growing string.

## Approach

Use a 26-dimensional column vector to record the count of each character. Build the transition matrix M: for a..y, one copy contributes to the next letter; one copy of z contributes to both a and b. After each round the vector becomes M times the previous vector, so after t rounds it is M^t times the initial vector. Use binary fast exponentiation, and finally sum the 26 counts and take the remainder. The reference counts the input byte by byte without keeping the full word.

## Proof of correctness

In one transformation, different original characters contribute independently and never merge with each other. All copies of the same letter have exactly the same descendants, so counting by character loses no information needed for the length. Column j of the matrix is exactly the count of what letter j produces in one round of simultaneous transformation, and matrix multiplication weights the columns and adds them up, which is the total contribution of all original characters, so one transition step is correct.

By induction, repeating t rounds gives M^t times the initial count vector. Fast exponentiation maintains the binary powers not yet used and the product of the powers chosen so far: whenever a set bit is read it is multiplied in, then the exponent is shifted and the base squared, and at termination the product is M^t. When t=0 the result matrix is the identity, so the original length is output. The final sum of the letter counts is exactly the total length of the transformed string; addition and multiplication are compatible with taking remainders, so reducing midway does not change the final remainder. For the empty string the initial vector is all zeros and remains zero after any number of rounds.

## Complexity and integer safety

The alphabet size is fixed at 26, so the time is O(|word|+26³log(t+1)), which can also be written as O(|word|+log(t+1)) for a fixed alphabet; the space is O(26²), and neither the input string nor the expanded string is stored. The matrix entries are reduced right after every multiply-add; a single product plus the current remainder is less than (1000000007−1)²+1000000006, far below the signed 64-bit limit. The input counts are also bounded by the 32MiB byte budget. Multiplications must be computed in 64 bits; 32-bit intermediate results cannot be used.

## Independent verification

The small oracle builds the new string directly: in every round it walks the old string, appending ab for z and the successor for any other letter; it does not call the matrix algorithm. The native reference is actually run on 163 unique small inputs. In addition, all 2387 combinations over the alphabet abyz with length 0..4 and rounds 0..6 are expanded directly and cross-checked against an independent linear-recurrence oracle.

The large-round oracle does not use matrices: let f(s) be the length of a single a after s rounds, with f(0)..f(25)=1; after 26 rounds a becomes ab, and b behaves like a one round ahead, so f(s)=f(s−26)+f(s−25). It computes x^s modulo the polynomial x²⁶−x−1 quickly and takes the dot product of the resulting coefficients with the 26 initial values. A starting letter with index j has length f(t+j), and the lengths are summed weighted by the input frequencies. After each polynomial multiplication, terms are eliminated from high degree to low using x^26=x+1, an implementation independent of 26×26 matrix multiplication.

Two cases close to 32MiB use an all-a string with t=0 and a cyclic letter string with t=2147483647, respectively. The answer for the former is given directly by the length; for the latter the character frequencies are computed in closed form from the full periods and the remainder, checked against character-by-character counting, and then fed to the polynomial oracle. Small and medium cases cover z splitting, the round boundaries 25/26, the modulus, every single letter with a large number of rounds, the empty string and the full alphabet. Four negative controls that exit normally test an off-by-one in the number of rounds, dropping the b produced by z, a wrong modulus, and transforming the ab produced in the current round too early.
